description: Original concise study explanations and practice questions. No textbook text or files. Drafts require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.7: Characteristics of the Partnership
entries.title: Recognizing a general partnership
entries.summary: A partnership can arise from how people conduct a profit-making business together, even without a formal partnership agreement or filing. Analyze co-ownership through both economic participation and the power to share in significant management decisions. Profit sharing is evidence, not a complete substitute for the co-ownership inquiry. Keep entity treatment for particular legal purposes separate from the partners’ own liability.
entries.checklist: Identify two or more persons; a business for profit; co-ownership; profit participation and meaningful management power.
entries.question: Does sharing profits by itself establish a partnership?
entries.answer: No. It is evidence of partnership, but the co-ownership inquiry also examines the power to participate in significant management decisions.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.9: The Limited Partnership
entries.title: Limited partnerships and statutory formation
entries.summary: A limited partnership is a statutory business form, unlike a general partnership that may arise informally. The traditional structure separates general partners, who manage and face general-partner liability, from limited partners whose liability protection depends on the governing statute. Check the formation filing and applicable statutory version before treating an investor as protected.
entries.checklist: Check the governing limited-partnership statute, required certificate, partner classes and statutory liability provisions.
entries.question: What is the key formation difference between a general and limited partnership?
entries.answer: A limited partnership requires compliance with statutory formation formalities; an ordinary partnership may arise without a filing.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.11: The Limited Liability Company
entries.title: LLC ownership and operating agreements
entries.summary: An LLC is a statutory entity with members rather than corporate shareholders. Its operating agreement organizes the owners’ economic and management relationship. Limited liability and flexible governance are important features, but distribution rights, management rights and tax treatment are distinct questions. Do not infer that a share of profits necessarily gives a member an immediate right to demand a distribution.
entries.checklist: Identify members, applicable statute, operating agreement, management arrangement and distribution terms.
entries.question: Does an LLC member’s profit share automatically create a right to immediate distribution?
entries.answer: No. A right to share in profits is different from an enforceable right to demand that those profits be distributed.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.16: Public or Government Corporations
entries.title: Government corporations versus public companies
entries.summary: A government or public corporation performs a public function under public creation and control. That category is different from a publicly held business corporation whose shares trade among investors. Identify the kind of entity before applying private corporate-law assumptions; some government-created entities operate under a separate statutory framework.
entries.checklist: Distinguish government creation/control from public trading of business shares.
entries.question: Is a publicly traded company necessarily a government corporation?
entries.answer: No. Publicly traded describes its investor market; a government corporation is defined by public creation/control and public function.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.18: Charitable and Other Nonprofit Corporations
entries.title: Nonprofit corporate categories
entries.summary: Nonprofit corporations can pursue charitable, mutual-benefit or religious purposes under special statutes. The supplied text discusses a model framework distinguishing these categories and their regulation. Identify the organization’s purpose and governing nonprofit statute rather than treating every nonprofit like an ordinary business corporation.
entries.checklist: Identify charitable/public benefit, mutual benefit or religious purposes; then locate the governing nonprofit statute.
entries.question: Why classify the type of nonprofit before analyzing its governance?
entries.answer: Different nonprofit categories can be governed by different statutory requirements and degrees of regulation.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 1.24: Agency—Core Concepts
entries.title: Actual and apparent authority
entries.summary: Actual authority concerns what the agent reasonably understands the principal authorized, based on the principal’s manifestations to the agent. Apparent authority instead examines manifestations attributable to the principal that reach a third party. An agent cannot establish apparent authority merely by asserting that it exists. Identify whose communication supports the claimed authority.
entries.checklist: Actual: principal to agent. Apparent: principal to third party. Identify the act and the relevant manifestation.
entries.question: Whose manifestations distinguish actual from apparent authority?
entries.answer: Actual authority rests on the principal’s manifestations to the agent; apparent authority rests on manifestations attributable to the principal that reach the third party.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 8.10: Ratification of Unauthorized Contracts or Transactions
entries.title: Ratification of unauthorized corporate acts
entries.summary: A corporation may later adopt an agent’s unauthorized but lawful act when it has capacity to perform that act and the ratifying decision-maker could originally have authorized it. Ratification may be express or inferred from knowledgeable acceptance of benefits or other conduct treating the transaction as binding. Silence alone should not be treated as automatic ratification without the surrounding facts.
entries.checklist: Identify original authority, corporate capacity, the ratifier’s power, knowledge of facts, and express or implied adoption.
entries.question: Can ratification occur without a formal board vote?
entries.answer: It may be inferred from conduct such as knowledgeable acceptance of a transaction’s benefits, provided the person acting has ratifying authority.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 9.1: The Traditional Pattern of Corporate Governance
entries.title: The corporate governance structure
entries.summary: The traditional structure separates shareholders, directors and officers. Shareholders select directors; the board manages or supervises corporate affairs and appoints officers; officers execute the business’s policies. Certain fundamental transactions require shareholder approval under governing statutes. Ownership therefore does not make each shareholder an independent manager or agent of the corporation.
entries.checklist: Separate ownership, board supervision, officer execution and statutorily reserved shareholder decisions.
entries.question: Does owning corporate stock make a shareholder the day-to-day manager?
entries.answer: No. The traditional structure assigns management or supervision to the board and execution to officers, while shareholders exercise voting and other ownership rights.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 3.1: Selection of the Corporate Form
entries.title: Choosing an organizational form
entries.summary: Selection of a business form is a contextual planning problem. Consider the enterprise’s financing, ownership, management needs and the participants’ circumstances rather than assuming incorporation is always preferable. Closely held businesses may have several realistic choices, and changing needs can make a later conversion appropriate.
entries.checklist: Compare financing, management participation, liability, tax and changing business needs under applicable law.
entries.question: Why is entity selection not a one-factor liability question?
entries.answer: The form must fit ownership, financing, management, tax and other business needs, which may change over time.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 3.2: Selecting the State of Incorporation
entries.title: Selecting the state of incorporation
entries.summary: The incorporation jurisdiction supplies important internal corporate rules, including director duties and shareholder rights. Forming in another state can also require qualification and costs where the business actually operates. Compare the legal advantages of a jurisdiction with additional filing, tax and administration burdens; do not assume out-of-state incorporation removes local obligations.
entries.checklist: Identify the operating state, proposed incorporation law, foreign qualification and overlapping costs.
entries.question: Does incorporating elsewhere eliminate obligations in the operating state?
entries.answer: No. The business may still need to qualify and satisfy fees, taxes and other requirements where it operates.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 5.3: Liability of the Corporation on Pre-Incorporation Contracts
entries.title: The future corporation is not yet a principal
entries.summary: Before formation there is no existing corporation for a promoter to represent as its agent. Incorporation alone does not automatically make the new corporation liable for the promoter’s earlier contracts. Analyze the separate legal basis on which the corporation later becomes bound rather than treating formation itself as adoption.
entries.checklist: Ask whether the corporation existed, who signed, and what later conduct or statute supplies corporate liability.
entries.question: Does incorporation alone bind a company to every promoter contract?
entries.answer: No. Formation alone does not make it liable; a separate basis such as later adoption or a governing statute is needed.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 5.8: Promoters’ Liability After Corporation Adopts
entries.title: Adoption does not automatically release the promoter
entries.summary: Corporate adoption and a promoter’s release are separate questions. When a promoter personally contracted for a proposed corporation, the corporation’s later adoption ordinarily does not itself extinguish that liability. A novation or comparable agreement with the other contracting party is needed to substitute the corporation and release the promoter.
entries.checklist: Separate corporate adoption from promoter release; identify assent to a novation.
entries.question: Does corporate adoption of a pre-incorporation contract necessarily release the promoter?
entries.answer: No. Adoption may bind the corporation while leaving the promoter liable unless the contracting parties agree to a substitution or release.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 6.3: The De Facto Doctrine
entries.title: De facto corporation analysis
entries.summary: The traditional de facto doctrine can protect an imperfectly formed business under specified conditions, including an available incorporation statute, a good-faith formation effort, apparent compliance and use of corporate powers. The doctrine and its survival depend on the relevant statute and jurisdiction. It is not a universal cure for ignoring formation requirements.
entries.checklist: Check applicable law; good-faith formation effort; colorable compliance; exercise of corporate powers.
entries.question: Why must a de facto corporation argument begin with the governing jurisdiction?
entries.answer: The doctrine’s availability and requirements vary, and statutes may limit or eliminate it.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 6.5: Corporation by Estoppel
entries.title: Corporation by estoppel is transaction-specific
entries.summary: Estoppel may prevent a party from denying corporate existence in a particular dealing even when general de facto status is unavailable. It does not necessarily create a corporation for every purpose. Focus on the transaction, the parties’ dealings and the jurisdiction’s doctrine rather than labeling the entity fully valid.
entries.checklist: Identify the specific transaction, the party denying corporate status and the applicable estoppel rule.
entries.question: Does corporation by estoppel validate an entity for all purposes?
entries.answer: No. It can bar a particular challenge arising from a transaction without establishing general corporate status.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 7.4: Lack of Formality and Confusion of Affairs as Bases for Piercing the Corporate Veil
entries.title: Commingling and disregard of separateness
entries.summary: Veil-piercing analysis examines whether controlling owners actually respected the corporation as a separate business. Intermingled assets and affairs, diverted receipts and serious failures to observe formalities can support a challenge, depending on governing law and context. The issue is not simply that one shareholder controls the company.
entries.checklist: Identify intermingling, misuse of corporate property, ignored boundaries and creditor consequences.
entries.question: Why does commingling matter in veil-piercing analysis?
entries.answer: It can show that owners themselves disregarded the corporation’s separate business and property, supporting a jurisdiction-specific challenge to limited liability.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 7.6: Inadequate Capitalization as a Factor for Piercing the Veil
entries.title: Capital adequacy is a factor, not an automatic test
entries.summary: Capitalization may matter when evaluating whether the corporate form improperly shifts business risks to creditors, especially in tort and closely held settings. The text cautions against treating undercapitalization as a mechanical, standalone ground in every case. Analyze the business’s risks and other circumstances under the governing standard.
entries.checklist: Compare capital with business risks; identify other separateness factors and the relevant jurisdiction.
entries.question: Does low capitalization automatically justify piercing the veil?
entries.answer: No. It is a potentially important factor, but the doctrinal significance and need for other facts depend on the jurisdiction and context.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 16.5: The Nature of Shares and Share Certificates
entries.title: Shares versus share certificates
entries.summary: A share represents a legally defined interest in the corporation, with economic and governance rights supplied by the charter and law. A certificate is evidence of ownership rather than the interest itself. Distinguish the rights attached to the share from the document or electronic record used to evidence it.
entries.checklist: Identify charter/statutory rights, ownership interest and evidence of ownership.
entries.question: Is a share certificate the same thing as the underlying share?
entries.answer: No. The share is the ownership interest; the certificate is documentary evidence of that interest.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 16.6: Issuance, Creation, or Allotment of Shares
entries.title: Authorized, issued and outstanding shares
entries.summary: Authorization establishes the shares the charter permits. Issuance creates share interests in owners. Outstanding shares remain in shareholders’ hands; shares reacquired by the corporation may be treasury shares rather than outstanding shares. Keep these categories separate when calculating ownership or evaluating an issuance.
entries.checklist: Determine authorization, issuance, current holders, reacquisition and retirement.
entries.question: How do outstanding shares differ from authorized shares?
entries.answer: Authorized shares are permitted by the charter. Outstanding shares have been issued and remain in shareholders’ hands rather than being reacquired by the corporation.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 16.14: The Shareholders’ Preemptive Right
entries.title: Preemptive rights and dilution
entries.summary: A preemptive right can give an existing shareholder an opportunity to buy a proportionate part of a new issuance. Modern availability depends on the governing statute and charter; it should not be assumed. Analyze the right separately from fiduciary limits on abusive issuance or dilution.
entries.checklist: Check statutory default, charter provisions, scope of the proposed issuance and any distinct fiduciary issue.
entries.question: Do all shareholders automatically have preemptive rights?
entries.answer: No. The governing statute and charter determine whether such rights exist and how far they extend.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 9.5: Necessity for Board Action in a Lawfully Convened Meeting
entries.title: Directors ordinarily act as a board
entries.summary: Board authority is generally collective, not a collection of individual directors’ personal powers. Traditional valid action occurs at a duly convened meeting, subject to statutory alternatives and other applicable doctrines. Identify the required form of action before assuming that informal individual assent binds the corporation.
entries.checklist: Check meeting requirements, permitted written/informal action and any ratification issue.
entries.question: Does each director independently possess all powers assigned to the board?
entries.answer: No. The board ordinarily exercises its powers collectively, subject to statutory methods for taking action.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 9.8: Directors’ Meetings: Place, Call, Quorum, Votes, Disqualification by Interest
entries.title: Quorum and voting requirements
entries.summary: Meeting validity and approval are distinct steps. The supplied text describes a usual quorum based on a majority of the full board, subject to governing statutes, charter and bylaws. Determine whether enough directors could act and then whether the required vote approved the action. Do not substitute shareholder voting rules for board rules.
entries.checklist: Identify full board size, governing quorum rule, valid attendance and the required affirmative vote.
entries.question: Why separate quorum from the vote needed to approve a board action?
entries.answer: Quorum concerns the board’s ability to transact business; the voting requirement concerns whether a particular proposal passed.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 13.16: Cumulative Voting
entries.title: Cumulative voting and minority representation
entries.summary: Cumulative voting permits a shareholder to multiply shares by seats being filled and concentrate or distribute those votes. Its function is to facilitate minority board representation compared with straight voting. First establish that cumulative voting is available; then calculate the voting pool and allocation.
entries.checklist: Verify availability; compute shares multiplied by seats; decide allocation among candidates.
entries.question: What is the basic cumulative-voting calculation?
entries.answer: Multiply the shareholder’s shares by the number of directors to be elected; the resulting votes can be concentrated or distributed as the applicable rules permit.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 14.11: Dissolution for Deadlock
entries.title: Deadlock and dissolution
entries.summary: Deadlock can provide a statutory basis for judicial dissolution, but the required circumstances are jurisdiction-specific. The model provisions discussed in the text connect management deadlock with inability to resolve it and resulting injury or business impairment, and separately address prolonged shareholder failure to elect directors. Dissolution is a remedy analysis, not an automatic response to disagreement.
entries.checklist: Identify the statutory ground, decision-making impasse, inability to resolve it and relevant harm or duration.
entries.question: Does ordinary shareholder disagreement automatically require dissolution?
entries.answer: No. The governing statute’s deadlock requirements and available remedies must be established.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 14.12: Oppression; Protecting Reasonable Expectations
entries.title: Oppression in a closely held corporation
entries.summary: Close-company disputes can involve more than voting stalemate. Statutes and equitable doctrines may address fraud, illegality, mismanagement or oppression of minority owners. Because triggers and remedies differ by state, identify the particular protected interest and statutory test rather than assuming a single national reasonable-expectations formula.
entries.checklist: Identify control, alleged oppressive conduct, applicable statutory test and available remedy.
entries.question: Why is the state statute important in an oppression claim?
entries.answer: States differ in the conduct, ownership thresholds and remedies that support minority-owner relief.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 10.1: Liability for Imprudence and Honest Errors of Judgment: The “Business Judgment Rule”
entries.title: Business judgment rule versus duty of care
entries.summary: The duty of care states a conduct obligation; the business judgment rule concerns judicial review of business decisions. Courts generally resist substituting hindsight for a board’s protected judgment, while rationality, good faith and the decision process remain relevant. A bad business outcome alone is not the same thing as an actionable care violation.
entries.checklist: Separate the directors’ conduct standard from the standard of judicial review; examine process and disqualifying facts.
entries.question: Is the business judgment rule simply another name for the duty of care?
entries.answer: No. Care addresses director conduct; business-judgment review addresses when courts defer to a business decision.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 10.2: Standard of Care and Diligence
entries.title: Care is evaluated in context
entries.summary: The text describes an ordinarily prudent director in a comparable position and circumstances, rather than an abstract promise of business success. Consider the corporation’s situation, the director’s role and the attention reasonably required. A conduct breach and damages liability are separate inquiries, including causation and any applicable protection.
entries.checklist: Identify role, circumstances, expected care and attention, causation and governing liability rules.
entries.question: Does every departure from an ideal decision necessarily create damages liability?
entries.answer: No. The applicable conduct standard, judicial review, causation and statutory protections must be analyzed separately.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 10.12: Statutory Treatment of Transactions with Interested Officers and Directors
entries.title: Interested transactions and statutory safeguards
entries.summary: An interested director transaction is not resolved merely by spotting a conflict. The text explains statutory approaches involving disinterested approval, shareholder approval or fairness. Their exact effect depends on the statute; compliance should not be treated as an unconditional validation of every aspect of the transaction.
entries.checklist: Identify the interest, disclosure, approving decision-makers, statutory conditions and any remaining fairness inquiry.
entries.question: Does following a conflict-transaction approval procedure always eliminate all scrutiny?
entries.answer: Not necessarily. The governing statute determines the procedure’s effect, and additional fairness or fiduciary scrutiny may remain.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed., § 11.8: Misappropriation of Corporate Opportunities: Disloyal Diversion of Business
entries.title: Corporate opportunities
entries.summary: A fiduciary may not exploit a position or confidential corporate knowledge to divert an opportunity belonging to the firm for personal benefit. The difficult inquiry is whether the opportunity is sufficiently connected to the corporation and what the relevant jurisdiction requires. Separate the opportunity question from whether the fiduciary disclosed it or obtained valid rejection/approval.
entries.checklist: Identify fiduciary role, connection to corporate business, use of position or information and applicable opportunity test.
entries.question: Why can taking an opportunity raise a loyalty issue even without a completed corporate contract?
entries.answer: The corporation may have a protected claim to opportunities sufficiently connected to its business and the fiduciary’s position or information.
entries.scope: Matches the fifth edition named in the supplied outline; jurisdiction-specific rules still require review.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 4; EPUB spine 17 · OEBPS/section15.xhtml
entries.title: Gideon and appointed counsel
entries.summary: The reproduced Gideon opinion rejects treating the ability to hire a lawyer as a prerequisite to a fair state felony trial. Identify the proceeding, indigency and the right-to-counsel rule before extending the result to other stages or categories of cases. The chapter discusses additional boundaries; this short outline is not a rule that counsel is appointed in every encounter with law enforcement.
entries.checklist: Identify stage of proceedings, seriousness of charge, indigency and the specific right invoked.
entries.question: What did Gideon establish in the state felony-trial setting?
entries.answer: An indigent defendant’s right to appointed counsel is fundamental to the fairness of a state felony trial.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 10; EPUB spine 24 · OEBPS/section22.xhtml
entries.title: Reliability of suggestive identification evidence
entries.summary: The Manson discussion treats reliability as central when applying the due-process identification doctrine. Relevant factors include viewing opportunity, attention, prior description, confrontation certainty and elapsed time, weighed against the procedure’s suggestive effect. Keep the threshold question about improper police-arranged suggestion separate from this reliability assessment.
entries.checklist: First identify the due-process threshold; then assess reliability factors and the corrupting effect of suggestion.
entries.question: Which reliability factors are discussed in the Manson/Biggers framework?
entries.answer: Viewing opportunity, degree of attention, prior-description accuracy, certainty at confrontation and elapsed time, assessed against the suggestive procedure.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 10; EPUB spine 24 · OEBPS/section22.xhtml
entries.title: Perry: identify the police-arrangement threshold
entries.summary: The casebook’s Perry discussion distinguishes an identification arising by happenstance from one arranged through improper police suggestion. Do not automatically apply a special due-process reliability screening merely because circumstances were suggestive. Identify police involvement before moving to the reliability factors.
entries.checklist: Identify how the confrontation arose and whether the police arranged the relevant suggestion.
entries.question: Why does Perry require attention to how an identification occurred?
entries.answer: The special due-process screening discussed there addresses improper police-arranged suggestive circumstances, not every suggestive encounter.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 6; EPUB spine 20 · OEBPS/section18.xhtml
entries.title: Katz and privacy-based search analysis
entries.summary: Fourth Amendment analysis asks whether government conduct intrudes on a protected privacy interest; technological observation and physical access require close attention to what was exposed and what remained private. The supplied discussion describes the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy approach and emphasizes protection of the home. This does not eliminate other recognized approaches to identifying a search.
entries.checklist: Identify government conduct, the interest invaded, exposure to others and the location or technology involved.
entries.question: What does a reasonable-expectation-of-privacy inquiry focus on?
entries.answer: Whether the asserted privacy interest is one society recognizes as reasonable in the context of the government conduct.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 6; EPUB spine 20 · OEBPS/section18.xhtml
entries.title: Probable cause and the totality of circumstances
entries.summary: The Gates discussion uses a practical, contextual assessment of probabilities rather than a rigid checklist for informant information. Consider what the facts collectively establish about evidence or wrongdoing, including the basis and reliability of information. Probable cause is not certainty or the trial standard of proof.
entries.checklist: Consider the combined facts, information quality, corroboration and the practical probability being assessed.
entries.question: Does probable cause demand rigid satisfaction of separate informant tests?
entries.answer: The Gates approach evaluates the totality of the circumstances as a practical assessment of probability.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 7; EPUB spine 21 · OEBPS/section19.xhtml
entries.title: Terry: the protective frisk is a separate inquiry
entries.summary: A protective frisk is a limited weapons search justified by a reasonable concern that the person is armed and dangerous, not an automatic evidence search following every investigative stop. Separate the justification for detaining someone from the justification and permissible scope of the frisk.
entries.checklist: Analyze the stop separately, then the safety facts and the limited weapons-search scope.
entries.question: Does a lawful investigative stop automatically authorize a frisk?
entries.answer: No. A protective frisk needs a separate basis to suspect that the person is armed and dangerous and remains limited by its safety purpose.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 7; EPUB spine 21 · OEBPS/section19.xhtml
entries.title: Vehicle search incident to arrest under Gant
entries.summary: A recent occupant’s arrest does not by itself authorize a routine search of the passenger compartment. The casebook discusses both access-related concerns and a vehicle-specific basis when evidence relevant to the arrest offense may reasonably be found there. Identify which rationale is actually supported; do not equate every traffic arrest with an evidence search.
entries.checklist: Check the arrestee’s access at search time and whether offense-related evidence may reasonably be in the vehicle.
entries.question: What are the distinct rationales considered for a Gant vehicle search?
entries.answer: Access by an unsecured arrestee within reaching distance, or the vehicle-specific reasonable basis to seek evidence of the offense of arrest.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 7; EPUB spine 21 · OEBPS/section19.xhtml
entries.title: Voluntary consent
entries.summary: Consent is not merely a spoken yes. The reproduced Schneckloth discussion assesses voluntariness from the circumstances and distinguishes actual choice from duress or coercion. Knowledge of a right to refuse is relevant, but the opinion does not make proof of such knowledge an invariable prerequisite. Authority to consent and the search’s scope remain additional issues.
entries.checklist: Assess circumstances, coercion, knowledge as a factor, authority and scope.
entries.question: Is knowledge of the right to refuse always a prerequisite to voluntary consent?
entries.answer: The Schneckloth discussion treats knowledge as a factor in the circumstances, not an invariable prerequisite.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 8; EPUB spine 22 · OEBPS/section20.xhtml
entries.title: Entrapment: subjective and objective approaches
entries.summary: The text distinguishes a subjective approach centered on government inducement and the defendant’s predisposition from an objective approach focused on unacceptable government conduct. Identify which approach governs before treating government participation alone as a defense. These approaches ask different questions and are not interchangeable.
entries.checklist: Identify governing approach; analyze inducement/predisposition or the prescribed government-conduct standard.
entries.question: How do subjective and objective entrapment approaches differ?
entries.answer: The subjective approach considers the defendant’s predisposition and government inducement; the objective approach focuses on whether government conduct goes too far.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 12; EPUB spine 26 · OEBPS/section24.xhtml
entries.title: Derivative evidence and an independent source
entries.summary: The Wong Sun discussion illustrates that exclusion can reach evidence derived from unlawful conduct, not just the immediate physical item seized. It also distinguishes knowledge obtained independently of the unlawful activity. Trace the causal chain and identify the particular doctrine that allegedly permits use of later evidence rather than assuming all later discoveries are automatically admissible or automatically excluded.
entries.checklist: Identify the illegality, evidence chain and whether the claimed independent source truly avoids that illegality.
entries.question: Why trace the source of later-discovered evidence?
entries.answer: Exclusion may reach derivative evidence, while genuinely independent acquisition presents a separate admissibility question.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 6; EPUB spine 20 · OEBPS/section18.xhtml
entries.title: Leon and objectively reasonable reliance
entries.summary: The good-faith discussion focuses on objective reliance and the exclusionary rule’s deterrent purpose. A magistrate’s error does not necessarily require suppressing evidence when officers reasonably obtain and execute a warrant. This is not a blanket exception for every warrant or for the officer’s subjective claim of good intentions; the surrounding circumstances and limits still matter.
entries.checklist: Identify the warrant process, the claimed error, officers’ objective conduct and the exception’s limits.
entries.question: Is an officer’s statement that they acted in good faith enough by itself?
entries.answer: No. The inquiry concerns objectively reasonable reliance and the doctrine’s limits, not merely subjective intentions.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 21; EPUB spine 37 · OEBPS/section35.xhtml
entries.title: Brady disclosure and materiality
entries.summary: The Bagley discussion builds on Brady’s concern with prosecution suppression of favorable, material evidence. Favorable evidence can include material useful for impeaching a government witness, not just directly exculpatory facts. Identify what was withheld, its favorable use and the applicable materiality analysis; a discovery-rule question and a due-process disclosure question are not always identical.
entries.checklist: Identify prosecution suppression, favorable use and materiality to guilt or punishment.
entries.question: Can impeachment information fall within Brady analysis?
entries.answer: Yes. The supplied Bagley discussion addresses the materiality of withheld information that could impeach government witnesses.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 9; EPUB spine 23 · OEBPS/section21.xhtml
entries.title: The privilege and custodial safeguards
entries.summary: The text describes protections against compelled self-incrimination and the particular concern posed by custodial interrogation. Distinguish the underlying constitutional privilege from the warning-and-waiver framework designed to protect it. A statement’s voluntariness and compliance with Miranda can require separate analysis.
entries.checklist: Identify compulsion, custody/interrogation where relevant, warnings, waiver and the doctrine governing admissibility.
entries.question: Are voluntariness and Miranda compliance identical inquiries?
entries.answer: No. They concern related but distinct protections, and the relevant statement may require analysis under both.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 9; EPUB spine 23 · OEBPS/section21.xhtml
entries.title: Interrogation under Innis
entries.summary: Miranda interrogation includes express questioning and its functional equivalent: police words or actions, beyond ordinary incidents of custody, that officers should recognize as reasonably likely to produce an incriminating response. Evaluate the circumstances from the suspect-oriented protection described in the opinion rather than relying only on an officer’s stated intent.
entries.checklist: First establish custody; then express questioning or its functional equivalent and any applicable exception.
entries.question: Can police conduct count as interrogation without a direct question?
entries.answer: Yes. Words or actions police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response may be the functional equivalent of questioning.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 9; EPUB spine 23 · OEBPS/section21.xhtml
entries.title: Warnings and waiver
entries.summary: The reproduced Miranda discussion identifies silence, potential use of statements, access to counsel and appointed counsel when appropriate as core warning subjects. The prosecution must establish the relevant warnings and waiver before relying on covered interrogation evidence. Do not infer a valid waiver solely from the existence of a printed waiver clause.
entries.checklist: Identify required warnings, understanding, voluntary choice and the specific waiver evidence.
entries.question: Does a printed acknowledgment alone resolve whether a waiver was knowing and intelligent?
entries.answer: No. The circumstances and actual waiver must be evaluated; a clause alone does not establish the required understanding and choice.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 20; EPUB spine 35 · OEBPS/section33.xhtml
entries.title: Barker speedy-trial balancing
entries.summary: The Barker discussion uses a contextual balance rather than a fixed constitutional stopwatch. Its factors are delay length, reason for delay, assertion of the right and prejudice. Delay length can trigger the fuller inquiry, while different reasons for delay receive different weight. Statutory deadlines are a separate issue.
entries.checklist: Assess length, reasons, assertion and prejudice together; distinguish constitutional and statutory rules.
entries.question: What are Barker’s four speedy-trial factors?
entries.answer: Length of delay, reasons for the delay, assertion of the right and prejudice to the defendant.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 26; EPUB spine 42 · OEBPS/section40.xhtml
entries.title: Attachment of jeopardy
entries.summary: The supplied discussion states the usual attachment points: a jury is empaneled and sworn in a jury trial, while the first witness is sworn in a bench trial. Attachment starts the analysis rather than deciding every mistrial or reprosecution question. Determine the procedural event before considering the doctrine governing a later prosecution.
entries.checklist: Identify trial type and attachment; then analyze termination, mistrial or later-prosecution issues separately.
entries.question: When does jeopardy ordinarily attach in jury and bench trials?
entries.answer: When the jury is empaneled and sworn, or when the first witness is sworn in a bench trial.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 22; EPUB spine 38 · OEBPS/section36.xhtml
entries.title: A valid guilty plea and waived trial rights
entries.summary: A guilty plea gives up important trial protections, including jury trial, confrontation and the privilege against self-incrimination. The discussion therefore requires a voluntary choice and knowing, intelligent waivers with sufficient awareness of relevant circumstances and likely consequences. Do not reduce the inquiry to whether the defendant merely said guilty.
entries.checklist: Identify voluntariness, understanding and the particular trial rights relinquished.
entries.question: Why must a plea inquiry address more than the defendant’s admission?
entries.answer: Because a guilty plea also relinquishes important constitutional trial protections, requiring voluntary and knowing, intelligent waivers.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 23; EPUB spine 39 · OEBPS/section37.xhtml
entries.title: Serious versus petty offenses and the jury right
entries.summary: The chapter explains that an offense authorizing more than six months of imprisonment is not petty for the jury-trial inquiry. A maximum of six months or less is presumptively petty, but sufficiently serious additional statutory penalties can matter. Use the authorized penalties, not merely the sentence eventually imposed.
entries.checklist: Identify maximum authorized incarceration and any sufficiently severe additional statutory penalties.
entries.question: Does a maximum sentence of six months or less end every jury-right inquiry?
entries.answer: No. It creates a petty-offense presumption, but sufficiently serious additional statutory penalties may rebut it.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 27; EPUB spine 43 · OEBPS/section41.xhtml
entries.title: Apprendi and sentence-increasing facts
entries.summary: The reproduced Apprendi rule generally reserves to the jury, using proof beyond a reasonable doubt, facts that increase punishment beyond the prescribed statutory maximum, apart from the stated prior-conviction exception. Identify the legally relevant ceiling and the fact increasing it; do not equate this inquiry with every fact a judge considers in sentencing.
entries.checklist: Identify the statutory maximum, the fact increasing it, who found the fact and the proof standard.
entries.question: What is the core Apprendi protection described in this source?
entries.answer: Apart from the stated prior-conviction exception, a fact raising punishment above the prescribed statutory maximum must be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Kamisar et al., Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 28; EPUB spine 44 · OEBPS/section42.xhtml
entries.title: Appeal rights need a specific source
entries.summary: The chapter distinguishes the absence of a general federal constitutional command that states create appellate review from constitutional constraints on systems that do provide it. Identify the statute or rule authorizing the appeal and the particular fairness or equality protection claimed. Direct appeal and collateral review are also different procedures.
entries.checklist: Identify the source and type of review and the particular constitutional protection at issue.
entries.question: Does the federal Constitution generally require states to create a criminal appeal?
entries.answer: The chapter says no general constitutional obligation creates the appeal itself; systems that provide review can still face specific constitutional requirements.
entries.scope: Supplemental casebook: this is not the assigned LaFave Criminal Procedure treatise, seventh edition.

entries.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 1 detailed notes; opening roadmap and foundational explanation
entries.title: Federalism and separation of powers
entries.summary: Federalism allocates power between federal and state governments; separation of powers divides authority among federal branches. The notes connect both structures with checks on concentrated governmental power. Treat supremacy as a rule about valid federal law, not an assertion that states have no sovereignty.
entries.checklist: Identify the level of government, branch and source of power.
entries.question: How does federalism differ from separation of powers?
entries.answer: Federalism concerns the federal-state allocation of power; separation of powers concerns divisions among branches.
entries.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not a textbook. Professor emphasis mentioned in those notes has not been independently verified.

entries.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 2 detailed notes; opening roadmap and foundational explanation
entries.title: Constitutional and statutory jurisdiction
entries.summary: Federal courts need authority within Article III and an applicable statutory grant. An important federal issue does not by itself supply jurisdiction. The notes distinguish original and appellate jurisdiction and connect judicial review to deciding actual disputes within these limits.
entries.checklist: Identify court, posture, Article III category, statutory authorization and case-or-controversy limits.
entries.question: Why is Article III alone not always enough for a lower federal court?
entries.answer: Federal judicial power must also be granted by an applicable jurisdictional statute within the constitutional boundaries.
entries.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not a textbook. Professor emphasis mentioned in those notes has not been independently verified.

entries.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 3 detailed notes; opening roadmap and foundational explanation
entries.title: Article III standing
entries.summary: Standing requires a personal injury that is concrete and particularized, actual or sufficiently imminent, traceable to the defendant, and likely to be redressed by the requested relief. The requested remedy matters: a past injury does not by itself demonstrate the future threat needed for an injunction.
entries.checklist: Analyze injury, traceability, redressability and each requested form of relief.
entries.question: Does a past injury automatically establish standing for an injunction?
entries.answer: No. Prospective relief also requires an adequately supported threat of future injury, with the other standing elements.
entries.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not a textbook. Professor emphasis mentioned in those notes has not been independently verified.

entries.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 5 detailed notes; opening roadmap and foundational explanation
entries.title: Separate threshold doctrines before the merits
entries.summary: Political question, adequate and independent state grounds, and state sovereign immunity ask different threshold questions. Identify the parties, forum, legal source and relief before choosing a doctrine. The notes caution against treating every politically sensitive dispute as nonjusticiable or every claim involving a state as identical.
entries.checklist: Identify who sues whom, where, under what law and for what relief.
entries.question: Why separate political question, state grounds and sovereign immunity?
entries.answer: They protect different structural interests and have different triggers; each must be analyzed under its own rule.

cases.locator: Macey, Moll & Hamilton, 14th ed., chapter 10, Shlensky v. Wrigley
cases.title: Shlensky v. Wrigley

fields.facts: A minority shareholder sought damages and installation of lights for night games at Wrigley Field, alleging that refusing night games harmed the Cubs financially.
fields.posture: Appeal from dismissal of an amended derivative complaint.
fields.issue: Did the pleaded objections to the directors’ refusal to install lights state a claim warranting judicial interference?
fields.reasoning: The alleged disagreement over business policy did not show the fraud, illegality or conflict-related basis for intervention discussed by the court; merely declining to follow other teams was insufficient.
fields.rule: Business-policy disagreement and a disappointing outcome do not alone establish a basis for judicial substitution of business judgment.
fields.significance: Separate business disagreement from pleaded facts that defeat deference. This is a supplied-edition case illustration, not a complete account of current director-liability law.

cases.locator: Macey, Moll & Hamilton, 14th ed., chapter 11, Marciano v. Nakash
cases.title: Marciano v. Nakash

fields.facts: Fifty-fifty owners disputed loans made to a deadlocked corporation by entities associated with one ownership faction. The loans had not obtained majority board or shareholder approval.
fields.posture: Appeal from validation of loan claims in the corporation’s liquidation.
fields.issue: Were the interested loans automatically voidable, or could full fairness support enforcement?
fields.holding: The court affirmed the finding that the loans were valid and enforceable because the fairness determination was supported.
fields.reasoning: The opinion rejected treating the absence of majority approval as automatic invalidity on these facts and examined the interested transactions for full fairness.
fields.rule: The supplied case illustrates substantive fairness review of an interested transaction rather than automatic invalidity based solely on the interest.
fields.significance: Spot the conflict, then identify the applicable statutory and substantive review framework. Do not treat a 1987 case as an unqualified statement of later statutory law.
